# Why hearts are missed

> DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

Unit D0 | Tier: Detect | Version 0.1

## You will be able to

- State how common congenital heart disease is and how much of it is found before birth.
- Name the two main ways a heart lesion is missed on a screening scan.
- Explain why the four-chamber view alone is not enough.
- List the features of a screening service that detects more.

## The size of the gap

Congenital heart disease affects about 8 in every 1000 live births and is a leading cause of illness and death in infancy. [1]

Detection before birth varies widely between regions and between lesions. Overall, fewer than half of cardiac anomalies are identified before birth. [2]


## You cannot screen by risk factor

A high proportion of the heart disease that could be detected before birth occurs in pregnancies with no risk factor and no other anomaly. The routine scan, done well on every patient, is what finds it. [3]


## Where the miss happens

In one retrospective study of missed diagnoses, views that did not meet technical criteria contributed to about half of the misses. In nearly a third, the view was technically adequate but the abnormal anatomy was not recognised. [4]

These are two different failures and they need two different habits. The first is fixed by obtaining every plane to a standard. The second is fixed by knowing exactly what normal looks like, so that anything else stands out. This course trains both.


## Why detection varies

Part of the variation is explained by the examiner's ability, transducer frequency, maternal body habitus, abdominal scars, gestational age, amniotic fluid volume and fetal position. [5]

Only some of these are in your hands. Skill and machine set-up are. Fetal position can often be dealt with by waiting or by bringing the patient back.


## Four chambers are not enough

The four-chamber and three-vessel views need much more than a count of structures. [6]

Some lesions, such as transposition of the great arteries and coarctation of the aorta, may not be evident in the four-chamber plane alone. Some lesions are not discovered until later in pregnancy. [7]

Adding the outflow-tract and great-vessel views raises detection of major malformations above the four-chamber view alone. It allows detection of tetralogy of Fallot, transposition, double-outlet right ventricle and truncus arteriosus. [8, 9]

Complete transposition, tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, common arterial trunk and pulmonary atresia with a ventricular septal defect can all have a four-chamber view that looks normal. They are typically abnormal in the three-vessel view. [10]

The same standard sweep can also pick up aortic and pulmonary valve stenosis, which may become more severe as pregnancy advances. [11]


## What a good screening service does

A screening programme performs better with continuous training based on feedback, a low threshold for referral for echocardiography, standardised protocols and easy access to fetal heart specialists. [12]

Each practice is encouraged to audit its stored images or clips against set quality criteria, to review its own detection rates and diagnostic accuracy every year, and to provide further training where needed. [13]


## What this course asks of you

Learn one sweep and do it the same way on every patient. Learn the criteria for each plane until a normal heart is boring. Drill on clips until a heart that is not normal catches your eye within a few beats. Refer early when a plane fails.

## Habits that close the gap

- [ ] Every patient gets the full sweep: situs, four-chamber, outflow tracts and great-vessel views [14]
- [ ] Each plane is judged against its criteria, not by counting structures [6]
- [ ] A normal four-chamber view is never taken as proof of a normal heart [7, 10]
- [ ] Low threshold to refer for fetal echocardiography [12, 15]
- [ ] Own images audited and detection reviewed every year [13]
